We learned yesterday that a judge allowed a $32 billion lawsuit alleging that the face recognition feature in Apple Photos violated a state privacy law to proceed.

This has constantly been conflated with Meta's use of face recognition, even though the two companies' practices sit at completely opposite ends of the privacy spectrum. In allowing the case to proceed, the court fundamentally misunderstood how this feature operates……

The Earlier Allegations Against Meta

To properly understand this situation, we need to start with a face recognition lawsuit against Meta that dates back to 2015.

Because that face recognition was performed on Meta's servers, and Meta could identify these faces, the company did violate the law and rightly was required to settle the claim for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under that same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which states that companies cannot collect biometric data without consent.

Apple's Approach Is Fundamentally Different

But there is a huge problem with this allegation: Apple absolutely does not collect biometric data to perform face recognition in the Apple Photos app. As the company noted in a machine learning research paper it published in 2021, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

Beyond that, all your iPhone does is tell you "these photos all contain the same person" — it has absolutely no idea who that person is. The only person capable of naming them is the iPhone user themselves.

The company's Photos privacy policy reflects this as well.

What I find truly unbelievable is that this lawsuit is already in its sixth year in the legal system, yet a few minutes of research would have revealed that its allegations are clearly erroneous.

Courts and legislatures should be actively praising Apple's approach to privacy, rather than conflating it with privacy-destroying practices from companies like Meta.

This is just another example of courts and legislatures fundamentally not understanding the technology they are trying to regulate. The most obvious example, of course, relates to end-to-end encryption. Multiple countries have threatened or attempted to ban end-to-end encryption, yet they have absolutely no concept of how encryption actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in every area they need to address. But they certainly have access to experts, and what I find truly baffling is that these lawsuits and legislative attempts have managed to proceed for years without anyone pointing out these fundamental fallacies, all the way to this point.
